pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 🌐 **Strand 3 — Communication Networks**
Sub-strand 4: Web Technologies

The World Wide Web is the world’s biggest library and classroom, but not everything on it is true. In this unit you will discover virtual learning environments and open learning websites, and learn how to judge whether a web page can be trusted.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B7.3.4.1** Demonstrate the use of a web browser (search engine).

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B7.3.4.1.1** Identify the importance of the web in learning (Virtual Learning Environments).
- **B7.3.4.1.2** Explore the use of open learning websites in the classroom.
- **B7.3.4.1.3** Demonstrate the techniques for evaluating web pages (accuracy, credibility, content, currency, functionality).

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 10.1 The Web in Learning: Virtual Learning Environments
- 10.2 Open Learning Websites
- 10.3 Evaluating Web Pages

**Core competencies developed:** Communication and Collaboration (CC6.1), Digital Literacy (DL5.1, DL6.3), Creativity and Innovation (CI5.4).

pages.title: The Web in Learning: Virtual Learning Environments
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.3.4.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain what a VLE is;
- explore the importance of VLEs for learning.
A **web browser** (e.g. Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, Safari, Opera) is software used to view web pages. A **search engine** (e.g. Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, Yahoo!) is a website that helps you find information on the web.
A **Virtual Learning Environment (VLE)**, also called a **Learning Management System (LMS)**, is an online platform that brings together the tools for teaching and learning: course materials, assignments, quizzes, discussion forums, grades and announcements.
| **VLE / LMS** | **Notes** |
|---|---|
| Google Classroom | Free with Google Workspace for Education; widely used in schools |
| Moodle | Free, open-source; used by many universities |
| Microsoft Teams for Education | Class teams, assignments and video lessons |
| Canvas, Schoology | Other popular LMSs used by schools and universities |
| iBox and iCampus (Ghana) | Developed by **CENDLOS** for Ghanaian schools; the iBox is an offline learning server that brings curriculum content to schools with poor Internet access |
## Importance of VLEs
- **Self-paced learning (e-learning):** learners study at their own speed, revisit lessons and catch up after absence.
- Create opportunities to **learn new skills without a regular classroom**, anywhere and any time.
- All materials are in **one place**, organised by topic.
- Teachers can give **instant feedback** through online quizzes and track progress.
- Supports **collaboration** through forums and group work.
- Learning continues during school closures (as in the COVID-19 period, 2020).
- Saves paper and printing costs.

pages.title: Open Learning Websites
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.3.4.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- identify open learning websites;
- explore their uses in the classroom.
**Open learning websites** provide free (or low-cost) courses, videos and exercises that anyone can use. Many contain **Open Educational Resources (OER)**, materials that are free to use and share.
| **Website** | **What it offers** | **Classroom use** |
|---|---|---|
| Khan Academy (khanacademy.org) | Free video lessons and practice exercises in Mathematics, Science, Computing and more; tracks progress | Practise algebra or watch a video on photosynthesis before a lesson |
| Coursera (coursera.org) | Courses from universities and companies; many can be audited free | Older learners and teachers take short courses (e.g. Python basics) |
| edX (edx.org) | University courses (e.g. Harvard’s CS50 Introduction to Computer Science) | Advanced learners explore programming |
| Saylor Academy (saylor.org) | Free self-paced courses with certificates | Self-study in business, IT and science |
| Code.org | Coding lessons and Hour of Code activities for beginners | Introduction to programming in the lab |
| BBC Bitesize, PhET | Revision notes and simulations | Revision and virtual experiments |
> 💻 **Practical session — Explore an open learning website**
1. Open a browser and go to www.khanacademy.org.
2. Search for **“Intro to computers”** or a topic you are studying in Mathematics.
3. Watch one video and complete the practice exercise.
4. Write a short paragraph explaining how this website could help learners in your class prepare for the BECE.

pages.title: Evaluating Web Pages
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.3.4.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- state the criteria for evaluating web pages;
- demonstrate the techniques for evaluating web pages.
Anyone can publish on the web, so some information is wrong, out of date, biased or even deliberately false (**misinformation** and **fake news**). Use these five criteria to evaluate any web page:
| **Criterion** | **Question to ask** | **What to look for** |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | How true is the information? | Facts can be checked in other reliable sources; there are references; no obvious spelling or factual errors |
| Credibility (Authority) | Who wrote the page? Is the person an expert in the subject? | Author’s name and qualifications; a reputable organisation; domain such as .gov.gh (government), .edu.gh (education), .org; contact details |
| Content (Relevance & objectivity) | Is it on the correct subject matter? Is it balanced? | Covers your topic in enough depth; facts separated from opinion; not mainly advertising |
| Currency (Current) | Is the content up to date? When was it last updated? | Date of publication or “last updated” date; links still work |
| Functionality | Does the site work well? | Pages load properly; links work; easy navigation; secure connection (https:// and padlock); no endless pop-ups |

pages.title: Evaluating Web Pages (continued)
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Worked example — Evaluating two pages about the BECE timetable**
Page A is on the **WAEC Ghana** official website (waecgh.org), dated this year, and lists the official timetable. Page B is a blog post with no author, dated three years ago, full of adverts, and asks you to “pay to see leaked questions”. Page A is **accurate, credible, relevant, current and functional**; Page B fails almost every test and is likely a scam.
> 💻 **Practical session — Web page evaluation checklist**
Choose two web pages on the same topic (e.g. “causes of malaria”). Score each page from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) on Accuracy, Credibility, Content, Currency and Functionality. Total the scores and explain which page you would trust and why.
